title: Active ETFs become a core wrapper for European wealth distribution
what_happened: GSAM launched its first European active UCITS ETFs in January 2025 (fixed income), an active equity range from 28 April 2025 (GQUS at 0.20% TER) and two more active fixed income ETFs on 24 April 2026. It says it launched 13 active ETFs in 2025 and has about $90bn of ETF assets globally.
client_effect: Wealth managers and model-portfolio builders can hold an active strategy in a wrapper that trades intraday, is easy to use on platforms and typically costs less than the equivalent mutual fund share class.
decision_that_changes: A fund selector now compares the same strategy across wrappers (SICAV share class vs ETF) and compares an active ETF against both index ETFs and traditional active funds.
existing_investments: Existing holdings in a mutual fund version may be switched into the ETF version, which moves assets rather than adding them and can lower the fee rate on those assets.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: lead with the wrapper the buyer's platform and portfolio process prefer; position low-tracking-error 'enhanced' ETFs as core building blocks for model portfolios.
sales_angle: Identify which gatekeepers have a mandate or model that can hold active ETFs, and whether the ETF is on the platforms their advisers use.
rm_angle: For clients already in the mutual fund, explain the differences honestly (cost, dealing, tax reporting, spread) and handle any switch so the client is not surprised by trading costs.
risks_counterarguments: Cannibalisation of higher-fee share classes; UK platform support for ETFs (fractional dealing, trading charges) is uneven; a low TER leaves little margin; low tracking error means outperformance, if any, is small.
client_question: Where an active ETF and a fund share class of the same strategy both exist, which would your portfolio process choose, and what on your platform decides that?
watch: European active ETF assets and flows; number of GS UCITS ETFs and their assets; whether UK platforms add ETF model portfolio functionality; TER moves by competitors.

title: Evergreen private-markets funds and ELTIF 2.0 reach the wealth channel
what_happened: Goldman Sachs Alternatives built a 'G-Series' of open-ended private-markets funds for qualified investors (G-PE launched 2 April 2025) and on 11 March 2026 added an ELTIF range starting with the G-European Credit ELTIF, its first evergreen product under ELTIF 2.0. G-Series funds are sold through GS Private Wealth Management and select third-party distributors.
client_effect: Private banks and wealth managers can offer private equity, private credit and infrastructure to eligible individuals with periodic subscriptions and limited redemptions instead of ten-year drawdown funds.
decision_that_changes: The distributor must decide whether clients are eligible and suitable, how large an illiquid sleeve can be, and whether its systems and advisers can handle periodic dealing and redemption limits.
existing_investments: Clients may fund the allocation from listed equity or bond funds, some of which may be the same manager's.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: pair the product with adviser education and clear liquidity terms; work through a dedicated alternatives-for-wealth specialist team alongside the TPW coverage person.
sales_angle: Find distributors with an approved private-markets allocation and the operational set-up to deal in semi-liquid funds; expect a long due-diligence process.
rm_angle: Keep advisers informed on valuation, redemption queue and gating terms before stress arrives, not after.
risks_counterarguments: Liquidity mismatch if many investors redeem together; valuation opacity; higher fees; suitability risk under the Consumer Duty; UK retail access differs from the EEA (ELTIF is an EEA label).
client_question: What share of a typical client portfolio could you put in assets that can only be redeemed quarterly, and who in your firm signs that off?
watch: G-Series assets if disclosed; redemption requests across the semi-liquid sector; FCA and ESMA statements on semi-liquid funds; number of distributors named in GS releases.

title: UK product disclosure is rewritten: Consumer Composite Investments regime
what_happened: The FCA published final CCI rules (PS25/20) on 8 December 2025. Firms can opt in from 6 April 2026 and the regime is fully in force from 8 June 2027. It applies to manufacturers and distributors.
client_effect: Advisers, platforms and investors will receive a redesigned product summary with a standardised core covering costs, risk and past performance.
decision_that_changes: Distributors must decide when to switch their systems to the new summaries and how they will present comparable cost figures across managers.
existing_investments: No change to holdings by itself, but clearer or differently calculated cost figures can change how an existing fund looks against peers.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: produce the new summaries early for the fund range sold in the UK and give distributors the data feeds they need.
sales_angle: Being operationally ready is a hygiene factor in due diligence; lateness can keep a fund off a platform.
rm_angle: Explain to existing distributors what changes in the documents their advisers hand to clients.
risks_counterarguments: Mostly an operational change; unlikely to win business; cross-border ranges must run UK and EU disclosure regimes side by side.
client_question: How are you planning the move to the new product summaries, and what do you need from fund managers before June 2027?
watch: FCA implementation updates; distributor data-template standards; how overseas (OFR) funds are treated.

title: Targeted support: a new way for UK firms to suggest investments without full advice
what_happened: The FCA's PS25/22 (December 2025) set near-final rules for 'targeted support', where firms give ready-made suggestions to groups of consumers with common characteristics. The FCA expected the rules to take effect from 6 April 2026.
client_effect: Platforms, banks and pension providers can point non-advised customers towards specific investment solutions, which may bring cash savers into funds.
decision_that_changes: A distributor decides whether to offer targeted support and which funds or portfolios sit behind each ready-made suggestion.
existing_investments: Limited direct effect; over time default-style multi-asset solutions may gather a larger share of new non-advised money.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: offer simple, low-cost building blocks or multi-asset funds that a distributor can defend as a ready-made suggestion under the Consumer Duty.
sales_angle: Ask distributors whether they will launch targeted support and how the underlying funds will be chosen.
rm_angle: Support distributors with the evidence they need to show the suggested product offers fair value for the segment.
risks_counterarguments: Distributors may use in-house or index funds; take-up may be slow; the FCA says consumers remain responsible for their decisions, so reputational risk is real if outcomes disappoint. Commencement on 6 April 2026 was not confirmed in this research session.
client_question: Are you planning a targeted support service, and if so how will you select what sits behind each suggestion?
watch: Which firms get the new permission; FCA data on take-up; whether suggestions favour in-house, passive or third-party funds.

title: Overseas Funds Regime decides how EEA-domiciled funds stay on sale in the UK
what_happened: The FCA's PS24/7 (July 2024) implemented the Overseas Funds Regime. EEA UCITS, except money-market funds, can apply for recognition to be marketed to UK retail investors, replacing the Temporary Marketing Permissions Regime.
client_effect: UK wealth managers and platforms can keep using Luxembourg and Irish UCITS and UCITS ETFs once recognised.
decision_that_changes: A fund selector needs to know each overseas fund has recognition; a manager must decide which funds are worth registering.
existing_investments: Funds not moved into the OFR can no longer be promoted to UK retail investors, which can force switches.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: ensure the cross-border range sold in the UK is recognised on time and tell distributors early about any fund that will not be.
sales_angle: Recognition status is a due-diligence item for any new UK platform listing.
rm_angle: Proactively confirm the status of each fund a client holds.
risks_counterarguments: Low-probability, high-impact operational risk; money-market funds are excluded from the first equivalence decision; the TMPR end date after any extension was not verified here.
client_question: Do any funds on your list face an OFR recognition question, and how are you handling them?
watch: FCA landing-slot timetable; any equivalence decision for money-market funds; UK-EU regulatory divergence.

title: Value-for-money scrutiny: Consumer Duty and annual assessments of value
what_happened: UK authorised fund managers have had to assess each fund's value at least annually since September 2019, and the Consumer Duty adds a 'price and value' outcome that distributors must also meet.
client_effect: Wealth managers must be able to show that the total cost a client pays, including the fund, is fair for what the client receives.
decision_that_changes: Fund selectors weigh fees more heavily and may remove funds whose cost they cannot justify, or switch to cheaper share classes, ETFs or index funds.
existing_investments: Higher-fee share classes face pressure to reprice or be replaced.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: offer institutional-priced share classes for scale, be explicit about what the active fee buys, and supply value evidence the distributor can file.
sales_angle: A credible answer on cost is needed before investment merits are heard.
rm_angle: Help existing distributors document value each year; raise share-class conversions before the client asks.
risks_counterarguments: Fee cuts reduce revenue on assets already held; cheapest is not always best value; a manager's own value assessment is not independent evidence.
client_question: When you last reviewed value across your buy list, what made a fund fail?
watch: FCA Consumer Duty reviews; published assessment-of-value outcomes; ETF TERs (GS active ETFs at 0.20%-0.25% are data points).

title: Fund tokenisation rules finalised in the UK
what_happened: The FCA published PS26/7 on 30 April 2026 with guidance for running fund registers on distributed ledger technology and optional rules for direct-to-fund dealing, effective immediately.
client_effect: Platforms and wealth managers may in time deal in fund units with faster settlement and fewer intermediaries.
decision_that_changes: Distributors decide whether their systems will support tokenised share classes; managers decide whether to launch them.
existing_investments: None immediately; tokenised share classes would sit alongside existing ones.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: pilot tokenised share classes where a distributor asks for them, most plausibly in money-market funds first.
sales_angle: Mostly a watching brief; relevant in conversations with platforms and digital wealth firms.
rm_angle: Explain what, if anything, changes for a client holding the conventional share class.
risks_counterarguments: Demand is unproven; operational and legal risk; benefits accrue mainly to the back office. Adoption levels were not researched in this stream.
client_question: Is tokenised fund dealing on your technology roadmap, or is it too early?
watch: Launches of tokenised UK authorised funds; platform announcements; FCA follow-up work.

title: Model portfolio services concentrate buying power in fewer hands
what_happened: A wealth manager's commentary reports the UK model portfolio service (MPS) market at about £190bn, up 32% year on year. More adviser money is run through centrally built model portfolios.
client_effect: Advisers outsource fund selection to a discretionary manager's model, so one investment team's decision moves money for thousands of end clients.
decision_that_changes: The decision moves from many individual advisers to a small number of MPS investment committees with tight cost budgets.
existing_investments: Funds held adviser-by-adviser can be sold when the client is moved into a model that does not hold them.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: cover MPS providers as institutional-style buyers, with low-cost building blocks, capacity and consistent data.
sales_angle: A single model inclusion can be worth more than many adviser meetings, but the bar on fees and due diligence is higher.
rm_angle: Inclusion can be reversed at any rebalance, so regular portfolio-manager access and honest performance explanation matter.
risks_counterarguments: The £190bn figure was seen only in a search result and its original source is unknown; MPS cost caps favour passive funds; concentration cuts both ways when a model drops a fund.
client_question: How much of your firm's new money now goes through models, and what cost budget does the model team work to?
watch: Primary MPS market data (find and cite the original provider); share of passive in MPS; platform MPS charges.

title: Consolidation and outside capital in UK advice and wealth firms
what_happened: On 28 January 2026 Goldman Sachs Alternatives agreed to take a minority stake in The Private Office, a UK financial planning firm with over £3bn of client funds, subject to FCA approval. It is one public example of institutional capital buying into UK advice firms.
client_effect: As advice firms merge or take private-equity backing they tend to centralise investment propositions and reduce the number of funds and managers used.
decision_that_changes: Fund selection moves to a central investment committee; acquired firms' legacy fund holdings are reviewed.
existing_investments: A fund held by an acquired firm can be removed when its clients are moved to the acquirer's central proposition.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: build relationships with consolidators' central investment teams early and offer scale pricing.
sales_angle: Map who decides after each deal; the adviser relationship that won the business may no longer control it.
rm_angle: Watch for ownership changes at existing clients and re-earn the position with the new decision-makers.
risks_counterarguments: The TPO deal is an investment by the Alternatives business and the release does not link it to fund distribution; wider consolidation data was not sourced in this session; a manager owning a stake in an adviser raises conflict-of-interest questions.
client_question: After your recent acquisitions, how are you bringing investment propositions together, and who now owns fund selection?
watch: Deal announcements; FCA commentary on consolidators; number of funds on consolidators' central lists.

title: Government push for a UK retail investment culture
what_happened: Budget 2025 (26 November 2025) announced reforms to ISAs as part of a wider strategy to develop a retail investment culture.
client_effect: More savers may be steered from cash into investments, mostly through platforms and banks.
decision_that_changes: Platforms and wealth managers decide what default or suggested investments to put in front of new investors.
existing_investments: Little direct effect on existing fund holdings.
possible_gsam_response: Layer B: simple multi-asset and core equity funds or ETFs that distributors can use for first-time investors.
sales_angle: Relevant to platform and bank distributors more than to private banks.
rm_angle: Not a relationship issue unless a distributor redesigns its ISA range.
risks_counterarguments: The specific ISA limits and dates were not read in the portions of the Budget document fetched, so do not quote numbers from this entry; behavioural response is uncertain; new money may go mainly to index funds.
client_question: Do you expect ISA changes to alter what your non-advised customers buy?
watch: Final ISA rules and dates; platform flow data; any later Budget changes before the cutoff.

title: Leadership change in GSAM's EMEA Third Party Wealth business
what_happened: Hilary Lopez, head of the EMEA Third Party Wealth business since 2021, left in spring 2026 and is reported to be joining BlackRock as head of European wealth. Trade press says the global TPW business continues under co-heads Padi Raphael and Bryon Lake. No EMEA successor was found.
client_effect: Distributors' senior contact changes; day-to-day coverage usually continues through country teams.
decision_that_changes: None directly; some distributors review a manager's commitment to the channel when leadership changes.
sales_angle: For a candidate: know who publicly leads the channel globally and do not name an EMEA head without checking for a newer announcement.
rm_angle: Shows why relationship knowledge has to sit with the institution, not one person.
risks_counterarguments: Destination reported by trade press, not confirmed by either firm in sources read; a successor may have been announced after the searches run here.
watch: Any GSAM announcement naming a new EMEA TPW head; changes to country heads.
